opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely admirable ambition, and in some ways they've already earned the right to talk that way. AlphaFold winning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry wasn't a fluke. It came out of a very deliberate culture: pick a scientific problem that matters, that has a clear benchmark, where the community agrees on what "solved" means, and then throw world-class engineering and compute at it for years. Not many organizations can sustain that kind of focus.

But my feelings are a bit mixed, and that's partly from having spent time inside Google and having many friends at DeepMind.

On the positive side, I think the "Nobel Prize" framing is a healthy counterweight to the industry's obsession with products and leaderboards. A lot of AI today is about who ships the next chatbot feature first. DeepMind's identity has always been: we're here to do science, and AI is the tool, maybe the ultimate tool, for accelerating science. I really respect that. It's also a great way to attract people who want their work to matter in fifty years, not just next quarter.

On the other hand, I have two reservations.

The first is that the problems where AI wins Nobel-level results so far are a particular kind. Protein structure prediction had decades of carefully curated data, the PDB, and a well-defined competition, CASP. Many of the most important open problems in science don't look like that. There's no clean dataset and no clear objective. So the question is whether the AlphaFold playbook generalizes, or whether we were lucky to find one problem that fit it perfectly. I suspect the next breakthroughs will need something closer to real understanding of the world: models that can form hypotheses, run experiments, see, and act. That's why I care so much about visual intelligence and world models. Language alone won't get you there.

The second is organizational. Since the merger with Google Brain, DeepMind also has to be Google's main engine for Gemini and for competing commercially. That's a huge pull. Even with the best intentions, when the whole company's fate depends on the frontier model race, long-horizon science gets squeezed. Talent, compute, and attention all flow toward the product. So I'm curious, honestly, whether the "multiple Nobel Prizes" vision can survive that pressure, or whether it becomes more of a brand than an operating principle.

So my view is: I hope they do it, and I think the world is better if at least one well-funded lab takes that goal seriously. But I'd also like to see that ambition spread beyond one company. Science shouldn't depend on whether a single corporate lab decides it's still a priority. Academia, open research, and smaller labs need to be part of that story too. Otherwise "AI for science" just means "AI for whatever the big companies find strategic."

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold’s Nobel gives DeepMind “the right to talk” about the ambition, suggesting some success, but does not frame the ambition as once seemingly fantastical.

r002.rationale: It describes DeepMind’s deliberate focus and years of engineering and compute, but not a transition of AlphaFold from an exploratory idea into an organized execution-focused project.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the Nobel for AlphaFold really reframed what that ambition means. When Demis first talked about it years ago, a lot of people in the field, honestly including me, heard it as a kind of grand marketing line. Now it looks less like a slogan and more like a strategy that actually paid off.

What I find interesting is what kind of company it reveals DeepMind to be. They never saw themselves purely as an AI lab. The mission was always "solve intelligence, then use it to solve everything else." So the Nobel was not a side effect, it was the point. AlphaFold is a very clear example: you take a problem that biologists cared about for fifty years, you bring in modern deep learning, and the result is recognized by the scientific community itself, not just by the AI community.

At the same time, I would say a few things. First, the Nobel was for a very specific scientific achievement, protein structure prediction. It was not a prize for AGI. I think it's important not to conflate those. Second, I think it reflects something about how DeepMind operates that is a bit different from most labs today. They were willing to put a strong team on a problem with no obvious product and no short-term commercial payoff. That kind of patience is rare, especially now that the whole industry is in a very intense race around large language models.

And honestly, that is where I feel some tension. The pressure on Google and on DeepMind to compete on Gemini is enormous. Doing science for science's sake, and doing frontier model competition, pull in different directions. Whether they can keep both going is an open question. If they can, then the ambition of winning more Nobel-level results is realistic, because there are many fields, materials, weather, mathematics, where the same recipe could work.

From my own perspective as a researcher, I think the lesson is less about prizes and more about taste. Picking the right problem matters as much as the method. AlphaFold won because they picked a problem that was well defined, had good data, and where success was unambiguous. That is a kind of research taste I think the field should learn from, regardless of who ends up getting the medal.

r001.rationale: The response says the ambition initially sounded like a grand marketing line, then AlphaFold’s Nobel made it look like a strategy that paid off, while calling further Nobel-level results realistic. This frames the award as an initial realization of the ambition.

r002.rationale: The response describes AlphaFold as a scientific achievement and mentions assigning a strong team to the problem, but does not describe a transition from an exploratory idea to an organized project focused on execution.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a powerful ambition. It says that the goal isn’t just to build a better product, but to use AI to make discoveries that really expand human knowledge. That’s a compelling way to bring talented people together.

But I would separate the ambition from the measure of success. A Nobel Prize recognizes a discovery after the fact; it isn’t necessarily a useful target for deciding what to work on every day. The more interesting question is whether you can build an environment where people consistently tackle important scientific problems and have the patience to pursue them.

So I take that ambition seriously. But ultimately, I’d judge it by the science it enables, including work that might never receive a prize.

r001.rationale: The response calls the Nobel ambition compelling and discusses how to judge it, but does not say that it has been partially realized or that it once seemed fantastical.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaFold or describe its development as moving from exploration to organized execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an inspiring ambition. It says that the goal isn’t just to build a better product, but to develop tools that can help us make fundamental discoveries. And with AlphaFold, you can see why people took that ambition seriously.

But I’d separate the ambition from the metric. A Nobel Prize recognizes a particular kind of contribution, often many years after the work happens. There are enormously important advances that won’t fit into that framework. So if the question is whether AI can help produce Nobel-level scientific breakthroughs, I’m optimistic. If the question is whether the number of Nobel Prizes is the right way to judge an AI lab, I’m much less sure.

For me, the interesting question is what happens after you solve one major scientific problem. Can you build methods that transfer to other problems? Can scientists use them to ask questions they couldn’t ask before? That would make the ambition much more meaningful than the prizes themselves.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold explains why people took the ambition seriously, but does not say DeepMind’s Nobel Prize success partially realized it or describe the ambition as once seemingly fantastical.
